source: Gobet (1993) A computer model of chess memory (CogSci): architecture
finding: First CHREST paper. Extends the EPAM-style discrimination net used in Simon and Gilmartin's MAPP with n-ary nodes, recursive chunking, redundant links, dynamic STM and a retrieval structure. Learning has two discrete steps: discrimination (add a test) and familiarisation (add features to a chunk).
numbers: Net of 3646 nodes after learning. Redundant links grew slowly: 4 after 100 positions, 10 after 1000, 14 after 2000, 20 at the end. STM about 7 symbols; about 20 fixations in a 5 s exposure.
limits: Implemented in LISP; Class A level only. MAPP baseline had a binary tree. Retrieval structure later judged inadequate.
agent_relevance: Blueprint for a memory of small recognised units with links: a discrimination-net index where learning only adds a test or adds detail.

source: Gobet (1993) CHREST: recall of random vs game positions
finding: CHREST reproduces the classic expert advantage on game positions over random positions.
numbers: Mean recall over last 100 tests: 10.66 pieces (sd 1.08) game vs 7.77 (sd 0.65) random; t(99)=21.92, p<.0001. Fit 97.4% of Class A data in Gobet and Simon exp 1b and 77.5% in exp 3 (multi-board recall).
limits: Model recalled random positions better than humans (7.7 pieces vs about 4). Author suggests emotion or basic memory limits. Model makes no inference errors.
agent_relevance: Recognition-based memory predicts a big gain on structured input and small gain on noise. Test our memory on shuffled versus coherent traces.

source: Gobet (1993) CHREST: mirror-image reflection simulation
finding: With the retrieval structure (internal board) available at recall, CHREST showed no mirror-reflection cost, unlike humans. Without it, the cost appeared.
numbers: With internal representation: F(3,33)=1.59, ns. Without: F(3,33)=2.868, p=.051; normal+horizontal vs vertical+central F(1,11)=7.34, p=.02. Fit 89.2% of Class A exp 2 and 93.7% of exp 1a. 17 positions per condition.
limits: Boundary condition: a uniform-weight board schema over-predicts robustness. Humans weight centre and king side more.
agent_relevance: A flat slot-memory can hide a chunk effect. Keep recognition (chunks) and schema (slots) as separate stores and test them separately.

source: Gobet (2001) Chunk hierarchies and retrieval structures: comments on Saariluoma and Laine
finding: Rival-model test. Saariluoma and Laine said a frequency-based correlation heuristic beats proximity-based chunking. Gobet re-ran CHREST on their data and argues it fits about as well; power and log curves fit game positions but not random positions.
numbers: Two human subjects trained on briefly shown positions; both rose fast then slowly (log or power curve) and slightly improved on random positions. CHREST learns chunks by spatial proximity.
limits: Only 2 subjects; no error or chunk-type data. Author says data cannot separate learning algorithms without chunk-structure and error data. The rival 'random neighbourhood' heuristic got worse as it learned more chunks.
agent_relevance: Two memory-building rules can fit the same curve. Do not credit a memory design from one fit; log what is stored and what errors appear.

source: Smith, Gobet and Lane (2009) Checking chess checks with chunks
finding: CHREST 3.0 beta simulated Saariluoma's (1984) check-detection task. Bigger learned networks gave faster decisions; chunks were assumed linked to extra knowledge (this pair is a check).
numbers: Human data: 2 beginners, 3 unrated, 2 experts (~2000 Elo), 1 GM; GM took about a third of the beginners' time (p<.001). Model: 60 positions, 20 subjects per network size 100/1k/10k/100k nodes. Exp 1 times 1705, 1403, 1301, 1068 ms (r2=0.92). Exp 2 (simplified perception) 1320, 1010, 883, 606 ms (r2=0.94). Chunk-match decision assumed 10 ms. Only 16,128 king+one-piece positions exist, so a ceiling is predicted.
limits: Human numbers read off a graph; only 8 humans; perception strategy was changed after seeing results (human intervention); 10% endgame training share was an estimate; model made no errors (humans 3.0%, max 4.1% for experts). Model fit better for advanced than novice players in exp 2.
agent_relevance: A cached recognition shortcut (known chunk gives an instant answer, else slow search) is a clean two-path design for our agent: look up first, search only on a miss.

source: Gobet et al. (2001) What forms the chunks in a subject's performance? Lessons from CHREST (BBS)
finding: A computational model used to count chunks. CHREST results in chess support Cowan's view of a visual STM of about 3 to 4 chunks; diagram learning shows several distinct chunk types.
numbers: Visual STM capacity about 3 to 4 chunks (BBS 24(1), 128-129).
limits: Only the abstract page was read; full text paywalled.
agent_relevance: Supports a small working set: hold about 3 to 4 recognised units, not a long list.

source: Lane and Gobet (2012) Using chunks to categorise chess positions (SGAI AI-2012)
finding: CHREST extended with templates and retrieval learning to classify chess positions by opening. Reported as matching a support-vector machine.
numbers: Accuracy equal to an SVM (exact figures not on the page I read). Pages 93-106.
limits: Abstract page only; no full text. No exact accuracies recorded.
agent_relevance: A chunk memory can act as a classifier of problem type, which is how our agent could pick an operator from past cases.

source: Bennett and Gobet (2025) Automatic adaptation to concept complexity (CogAct)
finding: Newest chunking model from Gobet's group. Learns concepts from raw data by chunking, attention and memory, across logic functions, artificial categories, literature, chess and music. Compared with a deep-learning model on individual music judgements.
numbers: No results on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Not stated whether the deep-learning comparator is an LLM.
agent_relevance: The chunk-model line is still active and aims at per-person concept spaces, a hook for user-specific memory.

source: Michaud and Jon-and (2024) Opening the black box of language acquisition
finding: A transparent architecture of sequence memory and chunking, trained by reinforcement learning, learns toy languages from scratch as an alternative to LLM pre-training.
numbers: No metrics on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; toy languages; no direct LLM benchmark.
agent_relevance: Chunking can serve as an interpretable memory layer instead of opaque weights.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: chess (ChessBench)
finding: Transformers trained on 10M Lichess games with Stockfish 16 labels (15 billion data points) play at grandmaster level with no search. Strength rises with model size.
numbers: Table 1: 9M model tournament Elo 2025, puzzle acc 88.9%; 136M Elo 2259, 94.5%; 270M Elo 2299, Lichess blitz 2895 vs humans, puzzles 95.4%. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct (PGN input) Lichess 1755 vs bots, puzzles 66.5%. AlphaZero policy only 56.1%, with 400 MCTS sims 95.6%. Leela 400 sims 99.6%.
limits: Supervised distillation of an engine; chunk theory is not tested. Huge data. Test boards are unseen, which rules out memorising them.
agent_relevance: Pattern memory at scale can match search on a narrow task. A prompt-only agent cannot copy it; only a large learned store reaches this level.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing LMs (COLM 2024)
finding: A GPT trained on real chess games (next-character) holds a board-state representation recoverable by linear probes. A skill vector added to activations raises or lowers play.
numbers: Legal move rate 99.8% (16 layer) and 99.6% (8 layer). Win rate vs Stockfish level 0 (about 1300 Elo): 64% (16L), 46% (8L). Probe accuracy per square 99.6% (16L) and 99.1% (8L) vs 74.7% and 75.0% for randomized models; Elo-class probe 90.5% and 88.6%. Table 3 (5000 games): standard board 69.6% to 72.3% with positive skill vector and 11.9% with negative; random-start boards 16.7% to 43.2% (2.6x).
limits: Shows an internal board state, not chunks. Pawn-deletion intervention had side effects on other pawns.
agent_relevance: A model keeps a latent state and a latent skill estimate, so a written trace may not be the memory it uses.

source: Karvonen (2024) random-board collapse as a machine analogue of the random-position effect
finding: The same models fell sharply when play started from 20 random moves, like the human collapse of chess recall on random boards.
numbers: Standard vs random board, no intervention: 16L 69.6% vs 16.7%; 8L 49.6% vs 15.7% (5000 games vs Stockfish level 0).
limits: This is play, not recall, and the author does not call it a chunk effect. The link to Chase and Simon is my inference.
agent_relevance: Memory tuned to typical structure fails on atypical input. Our schema should detect out-of-pattern states and switch off the fast path.

source: Toshniwal et al. (2022) Chess as a testbed for language model state tracking (AAAI)
finding: GPT-2-small LMs trained only on UCI move strings track pieces and predict legal moves with high accuracy given enough data. Extra board-state tokens help most on small data. Full game history (full attention) is needed.
numbers: Training sets 15K, 50K, 200K games. UCI+AP reaches 99.9 on the first column in Train-M and Train-L. Approximate-attention models score lower on one task: GPT2 w=50 69.5, Reformer 71.0, Performer 65.4, LSTM 60.2 vs GPT2 74.0.
limits: Table columns partly garbled in the PDF text, so I quote only unambiguous cells. Language-model chess, no humans.
agent_relevance: Explicit state tokens beat implicit tracking: a written board or state summary kept in context is a cheap external schema.

source: Schultz et al. (2024) Mastering board games by external and internal planning with LMs
finding: LLMs pretrained on domain data plus search reach grandmaster level with a human-like search budget. Strength grows with the log of test-time compute.
numbers: MAV model external Elo 2923 (mean scoring) and 2875 (max scoring). MAV with 100 MCTS simulations gains 68 internal Elo over searchless MAV. Games played: 14689 chess, 4480 Chess960, 2189 Connect Four, 6334 Hex.
limits: Needs training for domain knowledge; not a prompt scaffold; not a chunk test.
agent_relevance: A recognition prior plus a little search pays; fits the pattern-recognition theory of search (subfield 06).

source: Song et al. (2025) Beyond accuracy: geometric stability analysis of LLMs in chess evaluation
finding: Six frontier LLMs on about 3,000 positions evaluated standard boards well but many failed under rotation, which fixed-orientation pattern memory would predict.
numbers: Mean abs error vs Stockfish: Claude Sonnet 4.5 330 cp, GPT-5.1 362, Kimi K2 Turbo 394, DeepSeek Chat 443, Gemini 2.5 Flash 595, Grok 4-1-Fast 736. Rotation error: Claude 627, Kimi 726, DeepSeek 997, Gemini 855, GPT-5.1 2531, Grok 1047 cp. Average invariance error: Claude 280, Kimi 311, DeepSeek 402, Gemini 640, GPT-5.1 655, Grok 719.
limits: The 'pattern matching over spatial logic' reading is the authors' interpretation. Preprint; prompt details not checked.
agent_relevance: Fixed-orientation pattern memory is brittle under symmetry. Supports guardrail G3: test with a transformed input.

source: Walker and Lyons (2026) Chess-World-Model: 10M-game benchmark for exact state tracking
finding: Benchmark for exact board-state prediction from move sequences, with a held-out real-game split and a random-play out-of-distribution split. Recurrent models beat Transformers at 3M and 8M parameters. Real-game scores saturate above 18M; the random split stays discriminative up to 40M.
numbers: 10 million real games; sizes 3M, 8M, 18M, 40M; causal Transformer, SLiCE, Mamba-3, Gated DeltaNet.
limits: Small models, move-sequence input; no human comparison. Per-model accuracies not extracted.
agent_relevance: Random-play positions expose shortcuts from common positions: the machine form of the Chase and Simon random control.

source: Balogh and Jelasity (2026) Verification of the implicit world model via adversarial sequences (ICLR 2026)
finding: No chess sequence model tested is sound: valid adversarial move sequences force an illegal next move. Some recipes and datasets improve soundness. Board-state probes mostly have no causal role in next-token choice.
numbers: Models trained on random games and high-quality games with several recipes; none sound (counts not extracted).
limits: Abstract and introduction read; tables not read.
agent_relevance: A readable internal state is not a used state. Check outputs; do not trust a probe or a self-report.

source: Junkin and Nathanson (2025) Causal masking on spatial data: chess
finding: Models trained on spatial board states, even with causal masking, play stronger than models trained on move sequences.
numbers: Bidirectional vs causal attention on board vs move data; no figures extracted.
limits: Abstract read; strength numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Representing the position directly (the chunk-friendly view) beats the history; keep a current-state summary in the prompt.

source: Parfenova (2026) Do chess explanations reflect model decisions?
finding: On 200 Lichess endgame puzzles, explanations make a model's own move easy to recover, but with explicit moves masked they add little over the board alone. Random plausible explanations from other puzzles lower the probability of the correct move. Recognisable endgame motifs make moves easier to recover without making them more correct.
numbers: 200 endgame puzzles; effects small and decoder-dependent under strict masking.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: A recognised motif inflates fluent rationales without raising accuracy, so answers need code checks (G2).

source: Vo et al. (2026) Vision language models are biased (ICLR 2026)
finding: VLMs count familiar patterns from prior knowledge, not from the image. Domains include chess and game boards. Removing backgrounds nearly doubles accuracy.
numbers: Mean counting accuracy 17.05% across 7 domains; removing backgrounds +21.09 points; accuracy rises to about 40% with thinking tokens, then falls with overthinking.
limits: Visual tasks; chess is one of seven domains; per-domain value not extracted.
agent_relevance: A strong stored pattern overrides observation. Put the check outside the model: count with code.

source: Gong, Wan and Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study (AAAI-24)
finding: ChatGPT shows an n-back capacity limit like humans: sensitivity d' falls to about 1 at 3-back. Noise lowers performance; chain-of-thought and feedback prompts change results.
numbers: Verbal and spatial n-back, n=1,2,3; 50 letter blocks per n in the base verbal task; the CoT variant improved performance.
limits: Per-condition tables not all read. The link from n-back capacity to chunk limits is my inference.
agent_relevance: Prompt changes move the effective memory limit; test any working-set size on our own model.

source: Hu et al. (2024) HiAgent: hierarchical working memory management for long-horizon agent tasks
finding: An LLM agent uses subgoals as memory chunks. When a subgoal ends, its actions and observations are replaced by a summary. The paper cites Miller (1956) chunking and doubles success.
numbers: Success rate 42.00 vs 21.00 (+21.00 points) averaged over 5 long-horizon tasks. Jericho progress +23.94, steps -3.80, context -35.02%, time -19.42%. One task: +36.55 progress, steps -9.4, context -26.42%, time -22.42%. Ablations: one removed module cut success by 30 points; no trajectory retrieval cut success by 10 points.
limits: Chunk means a summarised subgoal block, not a learned CHREST chunk; no discrimination net. Five tasks from the authors' benchmark setup.
agent_relevance: The clearest case of chunking inside an LLM agent loop with measured gains. Supports subgoal-sized summary chunks in our memory.

source: Packer et al. (2023) MemGPT: LLMs as operating systems
finding: Tiered memory moves data between fast and slow stores to extend context, modelled on operating systems. Evaluated on document analysis and multi-session chat.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Paging, not chunk theory.
agent_relevance: An alternative memory design to compare with a chunk store; check cost and loss when summarising.

source: Feng et al. (2023) ChessGPT: bridging policy learning and language modeling (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: Combines game data and chess language in one dataset; releases ChessCLIP, ChessGPT and an evaluation framework for chess ability.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Pairing positions with natural-language annotation links chunks to labels, like CHREST's linked knowledge.

source: McIlroy-Young et al. (2020) Aligning superhuman AI with human behavior: Maia
finding: Engines do not predict human moves well. Maia, an AlphaZero-style net trained on human games, predicts human moves better and can be tuned to a skill level.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Not a chunk model.
agent_relevance: Skill-matched models suggest a memory built from cases at the user's tier, not from the strongest.

source: Chunk-count estimates quoted in Smith et al. (2009) and Gobet (1993)
finding: Estimates of expert chunk stores differ by a factor of three. Gobet (1993) says 50,000 chunks are needed for expertise (citing Simon and Gilmartin 1973). Smith et al. give 100,000 (Simon and Gilmartin) up to 300,000 (Gobet and Simon 2000) for a Grandmaster.
limits: Second-hand citations inside papers I opened; the original 1973 and 2000 papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Expert memory is large: tens to hundreds of thousands of units. A prompt cannot hold that; we need an external store with fast retrieval.

source: Gobet (2001) on the random-position skill effect
finding: Records a classic dispute. Chase and Simon found no skill effect on random positions; later reanalysis (Gobet and Simon 1996a,b) found a reliable but small one. Chunk theory predicts it because a large chunk database finds a few chunks even in random boards.
numbers: Small skill advantage on random positions; low statistical power cited for earlier null findings.
limits: Secondary statement in a commentary; the original numbers were not read.
agent_relevance: A null result can hide a small true effect through low power. Report effect sizes with N when we test the memory.
